headline_marked: [[Cristiano Ronaldo marries Georgina Rodriguez]] after a decade together in private ceremony in Portugal
headline: Cristiano Ronaldo marries Georgina Rodriguez after a decade together in private ceremony in Portugal
summary: The football superstar and his long-term partner tied the knot in a private family ceremony in Cascais, Portugal, a year after their engagement was announced. Their five children were present to celebrate the union.
details: Football icon Cristiano Ronaldo has officially married his long-term partner Georgina Rodriguez. The couple tied the knot in a private family ceremony held in the coastal town of Cascais, Portugal, a decade after they first met.

The news was confirmed by Ronaldo's representatives to AFP, stating that the event was "completely private and domestic." Their five children were present to witness the union, which comes exactly one year after their engagement was announced.

Ronaldo, 41, shared a subtle hint on social media, posting a picture of his hand over Georgina's, both wearing rings on their ring fingers. He captioned it with a heart emoji between the letters 'C' and 'G', signaling their new marital status.

The couple first met in 2016 when Georgina was working as a sales assistant at a Gucci showroom in Madrid. Georgina described it as "love at first sight," and they made their first public appearance together at the FIFA Best Football Awards in January 2017.

Their family includes Cristiano Jr. (born 2010), twins Eva Maria and Mateo (born 2017 via surrogate), and Alana Martina (born 2017 with Georgina). In 2022, Georgina gave birth to twins Bella and Angel, though Angel tragically passed away shortly after birth.

With over 750 million followers across social media, Ronaldo and Georgina are one of the world's most recognized celebrity couples, extending their influence beyond football into fashion brands and hotel chains.

headline_marked: [[SSC pass rate hits 19-year low]] at 62.25%, raising concerns over education system
headline: SSC pass rate hits 19-year low at 62.25%, raising concerns over education system
summary: This year's SSC and equivalent examinations recorded the lowest pass rate in 19 years, with 312 institutions seeing no students pass. This signals deep-rooted issues within the education system.
details: SSC results day often shows two contrasting realities: families celebrating success, and teenagers quietly worrying about failure. After nearly a decade of schooling, one exam result can feel like it defines their entire future.

This year, the SSC and equivalent examinations recorded a pass rate of 62.25 percent, the lowest in 19 years. This is a significant drop from 68.45 percent in 2025 and 83.04 percent in 2024. Even more concerning, 312 educational institutions had not a single student pass the exam.

These figures are not just statistics but warning signals from the education system. The issue reflects accumulated weaknesses throughout a child’s schooling, rather than solely individual student failure. Pass rates in English and mathematics, ranging from 66.64% to 81.29% and 69.61% to 83.34% respectively, highlight this problem.

Students do not suddenly become weak in these subjects in Class 10. Gaps in reading comprehension, language ability, numeracy, and problem-solving skills from primary school only widen as they progress. A few months of exam preparation cannot compensate for years of learning deficits.

A recent report by CPEIMU found many students in Dhaka, Narayanganj, and Munshiganj primary schools struggle with basic math and English instructions. This echoes a 2024 World Bank report, which stated 50 percent of students don't reach Minimum Proficiency Level by the end of Class 5. SSC failures are, to some extent, the final manifestation of these earlier problems.

Teachers bear significant responsibility, but blaming them alone is too simplistic. We must examine if schools have enough subject teachers, effective professional development, manageable classrooms, and strong leadership. Over half of the country’s 65,567 government primary schools lack a headteacher, and 13,500 assistant teacher posts are vacant.

Similar staffing issues exist in secondary schools, with 55 percent of high schools lacking headteachers. Such circumstances can lead to overworked teachers unable to provide adequate student support. Student attendance is also a critical factor, with economic pressures and loss of motivation weakening participation.

A BBS and Unicef survey last year showed a significant decline in student attendance from primary to secondary levels. While primary net attendance was 84.3 percent, it dropped to 59.6 percent in Classes 6-8 and 50.5 percent in Classes 9-10. These findings necessitate an investigation into the 312 institutions where no students passed this year.
